LINE, in its standard formulation, does not embed newly arrived cold-start vertices with zero observed edges by encoding raw textual node attributes with a neural network. LINE is a network embedding method for large-scale information networks that learns node representations from observed graph structure, specifically by preserving first-order and second-order proximity between vertices. Because its objective depends on observed links, a vertex with zero observed edges provides no structural signal for LINE to optimize against, so the method cannot natively infer an embedding for such a vertex from text alone.

If one wants to handle cold-start vertices with textual attributes, a common extension is to add a separate attribute encoder, such as a neural network that maps raw text into the same embedding space as LINE embeddings. In that hybrid design, the text encoder is trained to predict or approximate embeddings for vertices that do have graph context, and then is applied to unseen cold-start vertices to generate their node representations. This is an extrapolation beyond original LINE, not part of the original algorithm.

So the accurate answer is: LINE itself does not solve zero-edge cold start via textual neural encoding; a separate text-to-embedding model must be added to enable that capability.
